---
redu_schema: 2
repo: https://github.com/Forceu/Gokapi
plan:
  tool: deploy_compose
  image: f0rc3/gokapi:v2.2.4
  port: 53842
  vm: m1.medium
  flavor_id: "3"
  database: none (SQLite on the data volume; do NOT provision a managed database)
  hourly_cost_gbp: 0.0278
bootstrap:
  mcp: claude mcp add --transport http redu «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --client-id redu-mcp
  mcp_codex: codex mcp add redu --url «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --oauth-client-id redu-mcp
  source: gokapi
quirks:
  - "⛔⛔ THIS IS A PUBLIC FILE UPLOADER, SO SAY THE UNCOMFORTABLE PART TO THE USER BEFORE YOU DEPLOY IT. Everything shared from here is served from a hostname under *.redu.cloud, and a file host that strangers can write to becomes a malware and phishing host within days of being found. That is not a risk to the operator alone: a blocklisting of redu.cloud by a browser safe-browsing list or a mail provider lands on EVERY other customer with a hostname on that domain. THE OPERATOR IS RESPONSIBLE FOR WHAT IS UPLOADED, including anything uploaded through a file request they hand out. Gokapi is a good shape for this, because it has no self-registration at all, but the operator still owns the consequences of every account and every file request they create."
  - "⛔⛔ WHO BECOMES THE ADMINISTRATOR, AND WHEN: THE FIRST VISITOR WHO FINISHES THE ANONYMOUS INSTALL WIZARD, AND ON FIRST BOOT THAT WIZARD IS THE ONLY THING RUNNING. Verified at Setup.go:60-65 and :83-90: when the config file does not exist Gokapi starts a BLOCKING setup webserver, and its basicAuth wrapper returns early with NO authentication while isInitialSetup is true. Every other path answers 'Server is in maintenance mode, please try again in a few minutes.' (Setup.go:111). One anonymous POST to /setup/setupResult writes the entire configuration, creates the super-admin with a password of the caller's choosing, and shuts the wizard down (Setup.go:784-806 via Configuration.go:135-160). That is worse than an unclaimed signup form: the caller also chooses the database, the storage backend, the public URL and the encryption level. THERE IS NO ENVIRONMENT VARIABLE THAT CLOSES THIS. --deployment-password only EDITS an existing super-admin and then exits (Configuration.go:192-206), and the wizard runs before it (Main.go:56-63). CLOSE THE WINDOW AS PART OF THE DEPLOY with the claim script in the body of this file, and if the script fails, finish the wizard in a browser IMMEDIATELY or delete the deployment."
  - "⚠️ A HEALTHY CONTAINER DOES NOT MEAN A CONFIGURED GOKAPI. The image's own HEALTHCHECK (Dockerfile:24) is curl --fail against http://127.0.0.1:53842, and during setup mode that path returns HTTP 200 with the maintenance message. So the container reports healthy while the instance is unclaimed and world-open. Never treat the container health, or redu reporting the deployment ready, as evidence that setup is done. The claim script gates on the maintenance string itself, which is the honest signal."
  - "✅ THE GOOD NEWS, AND IT IS THE REASON THIS APP IS A REASONABLE PUBLIC UPLOADER: THERE IS NO SELF-REGISTRATION ROUTE AT ALL. Webserver.go:103-132 is the complete route table of the configured server and contains no /register, no /signup and no /setup. Accounts exist only because an admin created one on the /users page. Upstream's own README puts it the same way: only registered users can upload. So once the super-admin is claimed, the door is shut permanently and there is no registration setting to remember to turn off."
  - "THE ONE ANONYMOUS WRITE PATH IS A FILE REQUEST, AND IT IS OPT-IN TWICE OVER. Webserver.go:963-983: /publicUpload needs BOTH a valid file request id AND a matching key, compared in constant time, and it refuses once the request has expired or hit its file limit. The right to create one is a per-user permission, and Environment.go:70 defaults GOKAPI_GUEST_UPLOAD_BY_DEFAULT to false, so only users an admin grants it to can hand out an upload URL. TELL THE USER IT EXISTS, because handing out a file request URL is exactly the moment this becomes a world-writable uploader, and GOKAPI_MAX_FILES_GUESTUPLOAD (default 100) and GOKAPI_MAX_SIZE_GUESTUPLOAD (default 10240, which the source comments as 10 GB) are the two numbers that bound the damage. Both are far too generous for a 40 GB disk."
  - "⛔⛔ MOUNT /app/config OR EVERY REDEPLOY REOPENS THE ANONYMOUS SETUP WIZARD ON A PUBLIC HOSTNAME. This is the highest-value line in this file and it is the local form of the usual secret-a-redeploy-destroys trap. Configuration.go:38-41 decides whether to run setup by asking one question: does the config file exist? So a container whose /app/config is not a real volume comes back from any redeploy in first-run mode, unauthenticated, with the setup wizard open to the internet, while the uploaded files sit on the data volume. The same file also holds SaltAdmin and SaltFiles, generated once at setup (Setup.go:388-404, toConfiguration at :236-300), which are what the stored admin password hash and every password-protected download link are salted with, plus the encryption cipher if encryption is on. Lose the file and you lose the logins, the protected links and the encrypted files even if you somehow re-ran setup safely. Mount BOTH /app/config and /app/data as named volumes, and check it after boot: Setup.go:750-760 reads /proc/mounts and the wizard itself warns when either is missing."
  - "⛔ THE UPSTREAM COMPOSE PUBLISHES 127.0.0.1:53842:53842 AND ON redu THAT MEANS THE HOSTNAME NEVER WORKS. That binding is correct upstream, where the reverse proxy is on the same machine; on redu the proxy is elsewhere and connects to the VM, so a loopback-only publish leaves the public hostname answering 502 forever and looks exactly like a container that failed to start. Publish 53842:53842 instead. Also change the upstream image reference: it says :latest, which on this repository is a different digest from the newest version tag."
  - "⛔ THE PUBLIC URL HAS TO BE KNOWN BEFORE THE WIZARD IS POSTED. The 'Public Facing URL' is stored in the configuration at setup time (Setup.go:501-503, with a trailing slash added at :531) and it is what every download link is built from. Get it wrong and the links you hand out point somewhere else. Generate the dname yourself, in full gokapi-<8 lowercase alnum>.redu.cloud form, pass it to deploy_compose, and put https://<dname>/ into the wizard payload as the url field. Changing it afterwards means re-running setup with --reconfigure."
  - "⛔ DO NOT PROVISION A MANAGED DATABASE FOR THIS APP. Gokapi supports SQLite and Redis, and nothing else; there is no Postgres or MySQL provider in the tree. Upstream's own docs call SQLite fine for most deployments, and it is what this recipe uses, on the /app/data volume. Passing database:'managed' to deploy_compose would create a Postgres VM that Gokapi never opens a socket to and bill for it forever. Leave the database parameter at its default. Redis IS a supported alternative, but upstream warns that it needs persistence explicitly enabled or all data is lost on a Redis restart, and that the Redis password is stored in plain text in the configuration file; this recipe has not verified either against redu's managed Redis, so do not reach for it without telling the user that."
  - "⛔ READ THE DISK NUMBER BEFORE YOU SIZE THIS, NOT AFTER. Every shared file lives on the app VM, and the flavor disk is the entire budget: m1.small is 20 GB, m1.medium is 40 GB, m1.large is 80 GB. That is the WHOLE disk, before Ubuntu, dockerd, the image and the SQLite database. On a different redu deployment (425, a Nextcloud install) an m1.medium reported 32.4 GB free of its 40 GB once the OS and the app were on it; that is a measurement of a different app and only a rough guide here, but the shape is right, so plan on roughly three quarters of the flavor disk being usable. THE DEFAULT LIMIT MAKES THIS WORSE THAN IT LOOKS: Environment.go:47-49 defaults GOKAPI_MAX_FILESIZE to 102400, and the source comment says that is 100 GB, so out of the box one upload is allowed to be more than twice the whole disk. Set GOKAPI_MAX_FILESIZE to a number the user actually wants. GOKAPI_MIN_FREE_SPACE (default 400 MB) is the floor at which uploads start being refused, and 400 MB of headroom on a machine that also runs Docker is thin; raise it."
  - "EXPIRY IS THE OTHER HALF OF THE DISK STORY, AND IT IS THE POINT OF THIS APP. Gokapi's whole model is that a share expires after a number of downloads or days, set per upload. That is what keeps the disk from filling, so agree a sensible default with the user and say it in the handover, rather than leaving every share unlimited and discovering the disk full later."
  - "PORT 53842, FROM THE CONFIG AND THE ENVIRONMENT, NOT FROM AN EXPOSE. Environment.go:77 defaults GOKAPI_PORT to 53842 and the wizard writes the same value into the configuration, so both have to agree; the claim script posts port 53842 for exactly that reason. Pass 53842 to deploy_compose. There is no JSON health endpoint: before setup, GET / returns 200 with the maintenance string, and after setup GET /login returns the login page. Those two strings are the gate the scripts in this file use."
  - "SET TZ. Upstream's .env.dist sets TZ=UTC and their compose passes it through. It only affects timestamps and expiry display, but a share that says it expires at the wrong hour is a support question, so set it deliberately."
  - "LOGGED IP ADDRESSES: DECIDE, DO NOT DRIFT. The wizard's 'Save IP' option logs the DOWNLOADER's address, and upstream's own docs flag it as possibly not GDPR compliant. This recipe posts it OFF, which is the right default for an EU-hosted service, and it is a decision worth naming to the user rather than leaving implicit. Separately: Logging.go:44-54 automatically adds the Docker subnet to the trusted proxy list unless GOKAPI_DISABLE_DOCKER_TRUSTED_PROXY is set, and GOKAPI_TRUSTED_PROXIES (default 127.0.0.1) is the knob if the addresses in the log turn out to be the bridge gateway rather than real clients. That matters the day somebody has to answer an abuse report."
  - "CHANGING ANYTHING LATER IS --reconfigure, AND IT IS SAFE BY DESIGN. Run the container once with --reconfigure and Gokapi reopens the same wizard, this time behind HTTP basic auth with a random username and password PRINTED TO THE CONSOLE (Setup.go:68-79). On redu you read them with sudo docker logs on the app VM. Stop that container and restart the normal one afterwards; every user is logged out. Note this is also the only supported way to change the public URL, the auth method or the storage backend."
  - "SIZING IS AN ESTIMATE AND UPSTREAM PUBLISHES NO RAM FIGURE. Checked the README, docs/, the Dockerfile and the compose: there is no memory number to quote. m1.medium (2 vCPU / 4 GB) is reasoning from the shape of it, a statically linked Go binary on alpine whose main memory driver is GOKAPI_MAX_MEMORY_UPLOAD (50 MB by default) multiplied by GOKAPI_MAX_PARALLEL_UPLOADS (3), with anything larger spilled to a temporary file. m1.small would very likely run it; it is chosen against here for the DISK, not the RAM. Measure it on the first real run and write the number back into this file, because nobody upstream has published one."
  - "⚠️ plan_deploy WILL QUOTE m1.large ONCE needs_compose IS DECLARED. That larger floor exists for apps that BUILD from source; this one pulls a published image and it is a single small Go binary. Pass flavor_id '3' explicitly to hold m1.medium, exactly as deployment 420 did to save about 32 percent. Re-read the disk quirk first: m1.large is the right answer if and only if the user genuinely needs the 80 GB, and it is NOT trial eligible."
  - "DEPLOY: check_deploy_prerequisites -> plan_deploy (paste this file as redu_md) -> show the user the plan, the cost (about GBP 0.028/hr, roughly GBP 20 a month, with no managed database to pay for; fits the no-card free trial) AND THE DISK NUMBER, and WAIT for their yes -> generate the dname -> deploy_compose with flavor_id '3' (m1.medium), port 53842 and the database parameter left at its default. Then IMMEDIATELY run the claim script in the body of this file, before the URL goes anywhere."
  - "SOURCE IS UPLOAD MODE, NOT GIT. Nothing is built from source. Write the one-service docker-compose.yml from the body of this file locally, then prepare_upload -> run the returned tar and curl block -> deploy_compose with the source_token and no repo. # Self-host Gokapi on redu

A Firefox Send replacement you actually control: upload a file, hand out a link, and let it delete
itself after a set number of downloads or days. One small Go container, no database service, a
public HTTPS URL.

## What this deploys

- **Gokapi** from the official image, pinned, on one m1.medium VM, port 53842.
- **No database service.** Gokapi uses SQLite on its own data volume, so there is nothing managed
  to provision and nothing extra to pay for.
- Two volumes: `/app/config` (which is what keeps the setup wizard shut) and `/app/data` (the
  SQLite database and the files).
- A public hostname on `*.redu.cloud` with TLS.

About GBP 0.028/hour, roughly GBP 20 a month. Inside the no-card free trial. Delete it any time.

## Read this before anything else: it is a public uploader

A file host on a public hostname is a target. Left open, it becomes somebody's malware and
phishing host, and a blocklisting of `redu.cloud` by a safe-browsing list or a mail provider
lands on every other customer with a hostname on that domain. **Whoever operates it is
responsible for what is on it**, including anything uploaded through a file request they hand out.

Gokapi is a better shape for this than most, and the recipe leans on that:

| | Gokapi | What this recipe does |
|---|---|---|
| Self-signup | **does not exist**, there is no such route | nothing to close |
| Who can upload | only accounts an admin creates | one admin, created by you |
| Anonymous upload | only via a file request URL, with an id and a key | left off; the limits are named |
| First admin | **whoever finishes the setup wizard** | claimed by a script as part of the deploy |
| Max upload size | **100 GB by default** | set to a number that fits the disk |

## Read this before you size it: the disk is the constraint

Shared files live on the app VM. The flavor disk is your whole storage budget:

| Flavor | vCPU / RAM | Disk | GBP/hr | Trial |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| m1.small | 1 / 2 | **20 GB** | 0.0174 | yes |
| m1.medium | 2 / 4 | **40 GB** | 0.0278 | yes, at the ceiling |
| m1.large | 4 / 8 | **80 GB** | 0.0486 | **no** |

That is the whole disk, before Ubuntu, Docker, the image and the database. On another redu
deployment an m1.medium reported 32.4 GB free of its 40 GB after an app was installed on it, so
plan on roughly three quarters of the number in that column. Gokapi is picked at m1.medium for the
disk, not the memory: it is a single Go binary and would very likely run in 2 GB.

## Deploy

Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
directory containing this file:

    Read redu.md and deploy Gokapi on redu.

The agent shows you the plan, the cost and the disk number, and waits for your approval before
creating anything.

## The compose

Upstream's `docker-compose.yaml` pins `:latest` and publishes on `127.0.0.1`, which on redu
means the public hostname answers 502 forever. This is the same shape with a real version, a
reachable publish, named volumes and limits that fit the disk:

```yaml
services:
  gokapi:
    image: f0rc3/gokapi:v2.2.4
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - "53842:53842"
    environment:
      TZ: "${GOKAPI_TZ}"
      GOKAPI_PORT: "53842"
      GOKAPI_MAX_FILESIZE: "4096"
      GOKAPI_MAX_SIZE_GUESTUPLOAD: "1024"
      GOKAPI_MAX_FILES_GUESTUPLOAD: "10"
      GOKAPI_MIN_FREE_SPACE: "2048"
      GOKAPI_GUEST_UPLOAD_BY_DEFAULT: "false"
      GOKAPI_LOG_STDOUT: "true"
    volumes:
      - gokapi-config:/app/config
      - gokapi-data:/app/data
volumes:
  gokapi-config:
  gokapi-data:
```

`GOKAPI_MAX_FILESIZE` is in megabytes, so 4096 is a 4 GB ceiling per file. Pick a number with
the user; the default is 102400, which is 100 GB and more than twice the whole disk.
`GOKAPI_LOG_STDOUT` puts the log where `docker logs` can see it, which is where the
`--reconfigure` credentials appear later.

## The one that actually breaks it

**The first boot is an anonymous setup wizard.** Not a signup form: a wizard. Whoever completes it
chooses the database, the storage backend, the public URL, the encryption level **and** the
super-admin password. Until it is completed, every other path answers "Server is in maintenance
mode", and the container's own healthcheck reports the instance **healthy** the whole time.

There is no environment variable that closes this. `--deployment-password` only changes an
existing admin's password and then exits. The only thing that closes the window is completing the
wizard, which is why it is a script.

**And it can reopen.** Gokapi decides whether to run setup by asking whether its config file
exists. A redeploy without a real volume on `/app/config` comes back in first-run mode, wizard
open to the internet, with the files still sitting on the data volume.

## Claim the instance, and prove you did

Run this the moment the deploy reports ready, before the URL goes anywhere. Every field in the
payload was read out of `Setup.go` at tag v2.2.4; the wizard requires the keys for **all** auth
methods, not just the one being chosen, which is why the list is long.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Complete Gokapi's anonymous setup wizard and verify the result.
#   ./claim.sh gokapi-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud myusername
# Exit 0 = claimed and verified, 1 = FAILED (do not leave this instance up),
#          2 = inconclusive (it may still be starting; re-run).
set -eu
HOST="${1:?usage: claim.sh <host> <username>}"
GUSER="${2:?usage: claim.sh <host> <username>}"
TMP=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT

# 1. GATE. redu's proxy answers 502 for roughly the first 2.5 minutes while the container starts,
#    and an error page fails every assertion below in a way that reads like a pass. Require 200
#    AND require the string only an unconfigured Gokapi returns, before anything else runs.
code=$(curl -sSL -o "$TMP/root" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/")
if [ "$code" != "200" ]; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: / answered HTTP $code, not 200." >&2
  if [ "$code" = "502" ]; then
    echo "  502 is redu's proxy while the container starts. Wait and re-run. This is NOT a pass." >&2
  fi
  exit 2
fi
if ! grep -q 'maintenance mode' "$TMP/root"; then
  echo "FAIL: / returned 200 but not the setup-mode maintenance message." >&2
  echo "  Either somebody has ALREADY completed the wizard and owns this instance, or this is" >&2
  echo "  not Gokapi. Check by hand. Do not assume it is yours." >&2
  exit 1
fi
echo "OK: Gokapi is up and still in setup mode, so the wizard is unclaimed."

# 2. Confirm the wizard really is anonymous right now. 200 here is the POSITIVE result while
#    isInitialSetup is true; anything else means the state is not what this script expects.
scode=$(curl -sSL -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/setup/start")
[ "$scode" = "200" ] || { echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /setup/start answered $scode, expected 200." >&2; exit 2; }

# 3. CLAIM IT. Alphanumeric only, so there is nothing to escape in JSON or the shell.
#    The payload goes in from a file: an argument would show up in ps for every user here.
GPASS=[REDACTED:value] tr -dc 'A-Za-z0-9' < /dev/urandom | head -c 32)
cat > "$TMP/setup.json" <<EOF
[
 {"name":"dbtype_sel","value":"0"},
 {"name":"sqlite_location","value":"./data/gokapi.sqlite"},
 {"name":"redis_location","value":"127.0.0.1:6379"},
 {"name":"redis_prefix","value":""},
 {"name":"redis_user","value":""},
 {"name":"redis_password","value":""},
 {"name":"redis_ssl_sel","value":"0"},
 {"name":"authentication_sel","value":"0"},
 {"name":"auth_username","value":"$GUSER"},
 {"name":"auth_pw","value":"$GPASS"},
 {"name":"oauth_provider","value":""},
 {"name":"oauth_id","value":""},
 {"name":"oauth_secret","value":""},
 {"name":"oauth_recheck_interval","value":"12"},
 {"name":"oauth_admin_user","value":""},
 {"name":"oauth_only_registered_users","value":"0"},
 {"name":"oauth_restrict_groups","value":"0"},
 {"name":"oauth_allowed_groups","value":""},
 {"name":"oauth_scope_groups","value":""},
 {"name":"auth_header_admin","value":""},
 {"name":"auth_headerkey","value":""},
 {"name":"auth_header_only_registered_users","value":"0"},
 {"name":"port","value":"53842"},
 {"name":"localhost_sel","value":"0"},
 {"name":"public_name","value":"Gokapi"},
 {"name":"url","value":"https://$HOST/"},
 {"name":"url_redirection","value":"https://$HOST/login"},
 {"name":"ssl_sel","value":"0"},
 {"name":"logip_sel","value":"0"},
 {"name":"showfilename_sel","value":"0"},
 {"name":"storage_sel","value":"local"},
 {"name":"storage_sel_image","value":"local"},
 {"name":"storage_sel_proxy","value":"proxy"},
 {"name":"s3_bucket","value":""},
 {"name":"s3_region","value":""},
 {"name":"s3_api","value":""},
 {"name":"s3_secret","value":""},
 {"name":"s3_endpoint","value":""},
 {"name":"encrypt_sel","value":"0"},
 {"name":"enc_pw","value":""},
 {"name":"cleare2e","value":"0"}
]
EOF
code=$(curl -sS -o "$TMP/result" -w '%{http_code}' -X POST \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @"$TMP/setup.json" \
  "https://$HOST/setup/setupResult")
if [ "$code" != "200" ] || ! grep -q '"result": "OK"' "$TMP/result"; then
  echo "FAIL: the setup POST answered HTTP $code:" >&2
  cat "$TMP/result" >&2 || true
  echo >&2
  echo "  THE INSTANCE IS UNCLAIMED AND REACHABLE RIGHT NOW. Open https://$HOST/setup in a" >&2
  echo "  browser and finish the wizard THIS MINUTE, or delete the deployment. Gokapi answers" >&2
  echo "  with the name of the missing field, so a rejection here names what to add." >&2
  exit 1
fi
echo "OK: the wizard accepted the configuration."

# 4. The setup server shuts itself down about 1.5s later and the configured server starts.
#    Wait for it rather than guessing.
ready=0
for _ in $(seq 1 30); do
  sleep 3
  lcode=$(curl -sSL -o "$TMP/login" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/login" || true)
  if [ "$lcode" = "200" ] && grep -q 'csrf-token' "$TMP/login"; then ready=1; break; fi
done
[ "$ready" = "1" ] || { echo "INCONCLUSIVE: the configured server did not come up. Re-run." >&2; exit 2; }
echo "OK: the configured server is serving a login page."

# 5. PROVE THE OUTCOME, NOT THE STATUS CODE. A 200 from the wizard is not proof the password
#    works. A successful login answers 200 with a meta refresh to ./admin; a failure re-renders
#    the login form. The CSRF token is single use, so it is read from the page just fetched.
CSRF=$(sed -n 's/.*id="csrf-token"[^>]*value="\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p' "$TMP/login" | head -n1)
[ -n "$CSRF" ] || { echo "INCONCLUSIVE: no CSRF token in the login page." >&2; exit 2; }
code=$(curl -sS -o "$TMP/loggedin" -w '%{http_code}' -c "$TMP/jar" \
  --data-urlencode "username=$GUSER" --data-urlencode "password=[REDACTED:value]" \
  --data-urlencode "csrf-token=[REDACTED:value]" "https://$HOST/login")
if [ "$code" != "200" ] || ! grep -q 'URL=./admin' "$TMP/loggedin"; then
  echo "FAIL: signing in as $GUSER did not reach the admin page (HTTP $code)." >&2
  echo "  An account may exist with a credential you do not have. Do not leave this up." >&2
  exit 1
fi
echo "OK: signed in as $GUSER, so the account exists and the password works."

# 6. THE NEGATIVE HALF, which only means something because step 5 passed. The configured server
#    has no /setup route at all, so the wizard must now be gone.
scode=$(curl -sSL -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/setup/start")
if [ "$scode" = "200" ]; then
  echo "FAIL: /setup/start still answers 200. The wizard is STILL OPEN to anyone." >&2
  exit 1
fi
echo "OK: /setup/start is gone (HTTP $scode)."

echo
echo "CLAIMED. Admin user: $GUSER   (Gokapi lowercases it)"
echo "Password (shown once, store it now): $GPASS"
```

## Checking the volumes, which is what keeps the wizard shut

```bash
# On the VM, via get_ssh_command. Note redu's VMs run docker, not podman:
# a command that does not exist prints an error and greps to zero matches, which reads as a pass.
C=$(sudo docker ps --format '{{.Names}}' | grep -i gokapi | head -n1)
[ -n "$C" ] || { echo "no gokapi container found; nothing below means anything" >&2; exit 1; }

# Positive half: both mounts exist, and the config file that keeps setup closed is on one of them.
sudo docker inspect -f '{{range .Mounts}}{{.Destination}} {{end}}' "$C"
sudo docker exec "$C" ls -l /app/config/config.json /app/data/gokapi.sqlite

# Negative half: no database container is running alongside it. Only meaningful because the
# commands above just succeeded.
sudo docker ps --format '{{.Image}}' | grep -cE 'postgres|redis'

# And the number that decides whether this VM is the right size.
df -h /
```

# Self-host Gokapi on redu

A Firefox Send replacement you actually control: upload a file, hand out a link, and let it delete
itself after a set number of downloads or days. One small Go container, no database service, a
public HTTPS URL.

## What this deploys

- **Gokapi** from the official image, pinned, on one m1.medium VM, port 53842.
- **No database service.** Gokapi uses SQLite on its own data volume, so there is nothing managed
  to provision and nothing extra to pay for.
- Two volumes: `/app/config` (which is what keeps the setup wizard shut) and `/app/data` (the
  SQLite database and the files).
- A public hostname on `*.redu.cloud` with TLS.

About GBP 0.028/hour, roughly GBP 20 a month. Inside the no-card free trial. Delete it any time.

## Read this before anything else: it is a public uploader

A file host on a public hostname is a target. Left open, it becomes somebody's malware and
phishing host, and a blocklisting of `redu.cloud` by a safe-browsing list or a mail provider
lands on every other customer with a hostname on that domain. **Whoever operates it is
responsible for what is on it**, including anything uploaded through a file request they hand out.

Gokapi is a better shape for this than most, and the recipe leans on that:

| | Gokapi | What this recipe does |
|---|---|---|
| Self-signup | **does not exist**, there is no such route | nothing to close |
| Who can upload | only accounts an admin creates | one admin, created by you |
| Anonymous upload | only via a file request URL, with an id and a key | left off; the limits are named |
| First admin | **whoever finishes the setup wizard** | claimed by a script as part of the deploy |
| Max upload size | **100 GB by default** | set to a number that fits the disk |

## Read this before you size it: the disk is the constraint

Shared files live on the app VM. The flavor disk is your whole storage budget:

| Flavor | vCPU / RAM | Disk | GBP/hr | Trial |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| m1.small | 1 / 2 | **20 GB** | 0.0174 | yes |
| m1.medium | 2 / 4 | **40 GB** | 0.0278 | yes, at the ceiling |
| m1.large | 4 / 8 | **80 GB** | 0.0486 | **no** |

That is the whole disk, before Ubuntu, Docker, the image and the database. On another redu
deployment an m1.medium reported 32.4 GB free of its 40 GB after an app was installed on it, so
plan on roughly three quarters of the number in that column. Gokapi is picked at m1.medium for the
disk, not the memory: it is a single Go binary and would very likely run in 2 GB.

## Deploy

Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
directory containing this file:

    Read redu.md and deploy Gokapi on redu.

The agent shows you the plan, the cost and the disk number, and waits for your approval before
creating anything.

## The compose

Upstream's `docker-compose.yaml` pins `:latest` and publishes on `127.0.0.1`, which on redu
means the public hostname answers 502 forever. This is the same shape with a real version, a
reachable publish, named volumes and limits that fit the disk:

```yaml
services:
  gokapi:
    image: f0rc3/gokapi:v2.2.4
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - "53842:53842"
    environment:
      TZ: "${GOKAPI_TZ}"
      GOKAPI_PORT: "53842"
      GOKAPI_MAX_FILESIZE: "4096"
      GOKAPI_MAX_SIZE_GUESTUPLOAD: "1024"
      GOKAPI_MAX_FILES_GUESTUPLOAD: "10"
      GOKAPI_MIN_FREE_SPACE: "2048"
      GOKAPI_GUEST_UPLOAD_BY_DEFAULT: "false"
      GOKAPI_LOG_STDOUT: "true"
    volumes:
      - gokapi-config:/app/config
      - gokapi-data:/app/data
volumes:
  gokapi-config:
  gokapi-data:
```

`GOKAPI_MAX_FILESIZE` is in megabytes, so 4096 is a 4 GB ceiling per file. Pick a number with
the user; the default is 102400, which is 100 GB and more than twice the whole disk.
`GOKAPI_LOG_STDOUT` puts the log where `docker logs` can see it, which is where the
`--reconfigure` credentials appear later.

## The one that actually breaks it

**The first boot is an anonymous setup wizard.** Not a signup form: a wizard. Whoever completes it
chooses the database, the storage backend, the public URL, the encryption level **and** the
super-admin password. Until it is completed, every other path answers "Server is in maintenance
mode", and the container's own healthcheck reports the instance **healthy** the whole time.

There is no environment variable that closes this. `--deployment-password` only changes an
existing admin's password and then exits. The only thing that closes the window is completing the
wizard, which is why it is a script.

**And it can reopen.** Gokapi decides whether to run setup by asking whether its config file
exists. A redeploy without a real volume on `/app/config` comes back in first-run mode, wizard
open to the internet, with the files still sitting on the data volume.

## Claim the instance, and prove you did

Run this the moment the deploy reports ready, before the URL goes anywhere. Every field in the
payload was read out of `Setup.go` at tag v2.2.4; the wizard requires the keys for **all** auth
methods, not just the one being chosen, which is why the list is long.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Complete Gokapi's anonymous setup wizard and verify the result.
#   ./claim.sh gokapi-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud myusername
# Exit 0 = claimed and verified, 1 = FAILED (do not leave this instance up),
#          2 = inconclusive (it may still be starting; re-run).
set -eu
HOST="${1:?usage: claim.sh <host> <username>}"
GUSER="${2:?usage: claim.sh <host> <username>}"
TMP=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT

# 1. GATE. redu's proxy answers 502 for roughly the first 2.5 minutes while the container starts,
#    and an error page fails every assertion below in a way that reads like a pass. Require 200
#    AND require the string only an unconfigured Gokapi returns, before anything else runs.
code=$(curl -sSL -o "$TMP/root" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/")
if [ "$code" != "200" ]; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: / answered HTTP $code, not 200." >&2
  if [ "$code" = "502" ]; then
    echo "  502 is redu's proxy while the container starts. Wait and re-run. This is NOT a pass." >&2
  fi
  exit 2
fi
if ! grep -q 'maintenance mode' "$TMP/root"; then
  echo "FAIL: / returned 200 but not the setup-mode maintenance message." >&2
  echo "  Either somebody has ALREADY completed the wizard and owns this instance, or this is" >&2
  echo "  not Gokapi. Check by hand. Do not assume it is yours." >&2
  exit 1
fi
echo "OK: Gokapi is up and still in setup mode, so the wizard is unclaimed."

# 2. Confirm the wizard really is anonymous right now. 200 here is the POSITIVE result while
#    isInitialSetup is true; anything else means the state is not what this script expects.
scode=$(curl -sSL -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/setup/start")
[ "$scode" = "200" ] || { echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /setup/start answered $scode, expected 200." >&2; exit 2; }

# 3. CLAIM IT. Alphanumeric only, so there is nothing to escape in JSON or the shell.
#    The payload goes in from a file: an argument would show up in ps for every user here.
GPASS=[REDACTED:value] tr -dc 'A-Za-z0-9' < /dev/urandom | head -c 32)
cat > "$TMP/setup.json" <<EOF
[
 {"name":"dbtype_sel","value":"0"},
 {"name":"sqlite_location","value":"./data/gokapi.sqlite"},
 {"name":"redis_location","value":"127.0.0.1:6379"},
 {"name":"redis_prefix","value":""},
 {"name":"redis_user","value":""},
 {"name":"redis_password","value":""},
 {"name":"redis_ssl_sel","value":"0"},
 {"name":"authentication_sel","value":"0"},
 {"name":"auth_username","value":"$GUSER"},
 {"name":"auth_pw","value":"$GPASS"},
 {"name":"oauth_provider","value":""},
 {"name":"oauth_id","value":""},
 {"name":"oauth_secret","value":""},
 {"name":"oauth_recheck_interval","value":"12"},
 {"name":"oauth_admin_user","value":""},
 {"name":"oauth_only_registered_users","value":"0"},
 {"name":"oauth_restrict_groups","value":"0"},
 {"name":"oauth_allowed_groups","value":""},
 {"name":"oauth_scope_groups","value":""},
 {"name":"auth_header_admin","value":""},
 {"name":"auth_headerkey","value":""},
 {"name":"auth_header_only_registered_users","value":"0"},
 {"name":"port","value":"53842"},
 {"name":"localhost_sel","value":"0"},
 {"name":"public_name","value":"Gokapi"},
 {"name":"url","value":"https://$HOST/"},
 {"name":"url_redirection","value":"https://$HOST/login"},
 {"name":"ssl_sel","value":"0"},
 {"name":"logip_sel","value":"0"},
 {"name":"showfilename_sel","value":"0"},
 {"name":"storage_sel","value":"local"},
 {"name":"storage_sel_image","value":"local"},
 {"name":"storage_sel_proxy","value":"proxy"},
 {"name":"s3_bucket","value":""},
 {"name":"s3_region","value":""},
 {"name":"s3_api","value":""},
 {"name":"s3_secret","value":""},
 {"name":"s3_endpoint","value":""},
 {"name":"encrypt_sel","value":"0"},
 {"name":"enc_pw","value":""},
 {"name":"cleare2e","value":"0"}
]
EOF
code=$(curl -sS -o "$TMP/result" -w '%{http_code}' -X POST \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @"$TMP/setup.json" \
  "https://$HOST/setup/setupResult")
if [ "$code" != "200" ] || ! grep -q '"result": "OK"' "$TMP/result"; then
  echo "FAIL: the setup POST answered HTTP $code:" >&2
  cat "$TMP/result" >&2 || true
  echo >&2
  echo "  THE INSTANCE IS UNCLAIMED AND REACHABLE RIGHT NOW. Open https://$HOST/setup in a" >&2
  echo "  browser and finish the wizard THIS MINUTE, or delete the deployment. Gokapi answers" >&2
  echo "  with the name of the missing field, so a rejection here names what to add." >&2
  exit 1
fi
echo "OK: the wizard accepted the configuration."

# 4. The setup server shuts itself down about 1.5s later and the configured server starts.
#    Wait for it rather than guessing.
ready=0
for _ in $(seq 1 30); do
  sleep 3
  lcode=$(curl -sSL -o "$TMP/login" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/login" || true)
  if [ "$lcode" = "200" ] && grep -q 'csrf-token' "$TMP/login"; then ready=1; break; fi
done
[ "$ready" = "1" ] || { echo "INCONCLUSIVE: the configured server did not come up. Re-run." >&2; exit 2; }
echo "OK: the configured server is serving a login page."

# 5. PROVE THE OUTCOME, NOT THE STATUS CODE. A 200 from the wizard is not proof the password
#    works. A successful login answers 200 with a meta refresh to ./admin; a failure re-renders
#    the login form. The CSRF token is single use, so it is read from the page just fetched.
CSRF=$(sed -n 's/.*id="csrf-token"[^>]*value="\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p' "$TMP/login" | head -n1)
[ -n "$CSRF" ] || { echo "INCONCLUSIVE: no CSRF token in the login page." >&2; exit 2; }
code=$(curl -sS -o "$TMP/loggedin" -w '%{http_code}' -c "$TMP/jar" \
  --data-urlencode "username=$GUSER" --data-urlencode "password=[REDACTED:value]" \
  --data-urlencode "csrf-token=[REDACTED:value]" "https://$HOST/login")
if [ "$code" != "200" ] || ! grep -q 'URL=./admin' "$TMP/loggedin"; then
  echo "FAIL: signing in as $GUSER did not reach the admin page (HTTP $code)." >&2
  echo "  An account may exist with a credential you do not have. Do not leave this up." >&2
  exit 1
fi
echo "OK: signed in as $GUSER, so the account exists and the password works."

# 6. THE NEGATIVE HALF, which only means something because step 5 passed. The configured server
#    has no /setup route at all, so the wizard must now be gone.
scode=$(curl -sSL -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/setup/start")
if [ "$scode" = "200" ]; then
  echo "FAIL: /setup/start still answers 200. The wizard is STILL OPEN to anyone." >&2
  exit 1
fi
echo "OK: /setup/start is gone (HTTP $scode)."

echo
echo "CLAIMED. Admin user: $GUSER   (Gokapi lowercases it)"
echo "Password (shown once, store it now): $GPASS"
```

## Checking the volumes, which is what keeps the wizard shut

```bash
# On the VM, via get_ssh_command. Note redu's VMs run docker, not podman:
# a command that does not exist prints an error and greps to zero matches, which reads as a pass.
C=$(sudo docker ps --format '{{.Names}}' | grep -i gokapi | head -n1)
[ -n "$C" ] || { echo "no gokapi container found; nothing below means anything" >&2; exit 1; }

# Positive half: both mounts exist, and the config file that keeps setup closed is on one of them.
sudo docker inspect -f '{{range .Mounts}}{{.Destination}} {{end}}' "$C"
sudo docker exec "$C" ls -l /app/config/config.json /app/data/gokapi.sqlite

# Negative half: no database container is running alongside it. Only meaningful because the
# commands above just succeeded.
sudo docker ps --format '{{.Image}}' | grep -cE 'postgres|redis'

# And the number that decides whether this VM is the right size.
df -h /
```

Everything shared from here is served from a hostname under *.redu.cloud, and a file host that strangers can write to becomes a malware and phishing host within days of being found. That is not a risk to the operator alone: a blocklisting of redu.cloud by a browser safe-browsing list or a mail provider lands on EVERY other customer with a hostname on that domain. THE OPERATOR IS RESPONSIBLE FOR WHAT IS UPLOADED, including anything uploaded through a file request they hand out. Gokapi is a good shape for this, because it has no self-registration at all, but the operator still owns the consequences of every account and every file request they create."
  - "⛔⛔ WHO BECOMES THE ADMINISTRATOR, AND WHEN: THE FIRST VISITOR WHO FINISHES THE ANONYMOUS INSTALL WIZARD, AND ON FIRST BOOT THAT WIZARD IS THE ONLY THING RUNNING. Verified at Setup.go:60-65 and :83-90: when the config file does not exist Gokapi starts a BLOCKING setup webserver, and its basicAuth wrapper returns early with NO authentication while isInitialSetup is true. Every other path answers 'Server is in maintenance mode, please try again in a few minutes.' (Setup.go:111). One anonymous POST to /setup/setupResult writes the entire configuration, creates the super-admin with a password of the caller's choosing, and shuts the wizard down (Setup.go:784-806 via Configuration.go:135-160). That is worse than an unclaimed signup form: the caller also chooses the database, the storage backend, the public URL and the encryption level. THERE IS NO ENVIRONMENT VARIABLE THAT CLOSES THIS. --deployment-password only EDITS an existing super-admin and then exits (Configuration.go:192-206), and the wizard runs before it (Main.go:56-63). CLOSE THE WINDOW AS PART OF THE DEPLOY with the claim script in the body of this file, and if the script fails, finish the wizard in a browser IMMEDIATELY or delete the deployment."
  - "⚠️ A HEALTHY CONTAINER DOES NOT MEAN A CONFIGURED GOKAPI. The image's own HEALTHCHECK (Dockerfile:24) is curl --fail against http://127.0.0.1:53842, and during setup mode that path returns HTTP 200 with the maintenance message. So the container reports healthy while the instance is unclaimed and world-open. Never treat the container health, or redu reporting the deployment ready, as evidence that setup is done. The claim script gates on the maintenance string itself, which is the honest signal."
  - "✅ THE GOOD NEWS, AND IT IS THE REASON THIS APP IS A REASONABLE PUBLIC UPLOADER: THERE IS NO SELF-REGISTRATION ROUTE AT ALL. Webserver.go:103-132 is the complete route table of the configured server and contains no /register, no /signup and no /setup. Accounts exist only because an admin created one on the /users page. Upstream's own README puts it the same way: only registered users can upload. So once the super-admin is claimed, the door is shut permanently and there is no registration setting to remember to turn off."
  - "THE ONE ANONYMOUS WRITE PATH IS A FILE REQUEST, AND IT IS OPT-IN TWICE OVER. Webserver.go:963-983: /publicUpload needs BOTH a valid file request id AND a matching key, compared in constant time, and it refuses once the request has expired or hit its file limit. The right to create one is a per-user permission, and Environment.go:70 defaults GOKAPI_GUEST_UPLOAD_BY_DEFAULT to false, so only users an admin grants it to can hand out an upload URL. TELL THE USER IT EXISTS, because handing out a file request URL is exactly the moment this becomes a world-writable uploader, and GOKAPI_MAX_FILES_GUESTUPLOAD (default 100) and GOKAPI_MAX_SIZE_GUESTUPLOAD (default 10240, which the source comments as 10 GB) are the two numbers that bound the damage. # Self-host Gokapi on redu

A Firefox Send replacement you actually control: upload a file, hand out a link, and let it delete
itself after a set number of downloads or days. One small Go container, no database service, a
public HTTPS URL.

## What this deploys

- **Gokapi** from the official image, pinned, on one m1.medium VM, port 53842.
- **No database service.** Gokapi uses SQLite on its own data volume, so there is nothing managed
  to provision and nothing extra to pay for.
- Two volumes: `/app/config` (which is what keeps the setup wizard shut) and `/app/data` (the
  SQLite database and the files).
- A public hostname on `*.redu.cloud` with TLS.

About GBP 0.028/hour, roughly GBP 20 a month. Inside the no-card free trial. Delete it any time.

## Read this before anything else: it is a public uploader

A file host on a public hostname is a target. Left open, it becomes somebody's malware and
phishing host, and a blocklisting of `redu.cloud` by a safe-browsing list or a mail provider
lands on every other customer with a hostname on that domain. **Whoever operates it is
responsible for what is on it**, including anything uploaded through a file request they hand out.

Gokapi is a better shape for this than most, and the recipe leans on that:

| | Gokapi | What this recipe does |
|---|---|---|
| Self-signup | **does not exist**, there is no such route | nothing to close |
| Who can upload | only accounts an admin creates | one admin, created by you |
| Anonymous upload | only via a file request URL, with an id and a key | left off; the limits are named |
| First admin | **whoever finishes the setup wizard** | claimed by a script as part of the deploy |
| Max upload size | **100 GB by default** | set to a number that fits the disk |

## Read this before you size it: the disk is the constraint

Shared files live on the app VM. The flavor disk is your whole storage budget:

| Flavor | vCPU / RAM | Disk | GBP/hr | Trial |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| m1.small | 1 / 2 | **20 GB** | 0.0174 | yes |
| m1.medium | 2 / 4 | **40 GB** | 0.0278 | yes, at the ceiling |
| m1.large | 4 / 8 | **80 GB** | 0.0486 | **no** |

That is the whole disk, before Ubuntu, Docker, the image and the database. On another redu
deployment an m1.medium reported 32.4 GB free of its 40 GB after an app was installed on it, so
plan on roughly three quarters of the number in that column. Gokapi is picked at m1.medium for the
disk, not the memory: it is a single Go binary and would very likely run in 2 GB.

## Deploy

Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
directory containing this file:

    Read redu.md and deploy Gokapi on redu.

The agent shows you the plan, the cost and the disk number, and waits for your approval before
creating anything.

## The compose

Upstream's `docker-compose.yaml` pins `:latest` and publishes on `127.0.0.1`, which on redu
means the public hostname answers 502 forever. This is the same shape with a real version, a
reachable publish, named volumes and limits that fit the disk:

```yaml
services:
  gokapi:
    image: f0rc3/gokapi:v2.2.4
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - "53842:53842"
    environment:
      TZ: "${GOKAPI_TZ}"
      GOKAPI_PORT: "53842"
      GOKAPI_MAX_FILESIZE: "4096"
      GOKAPI_MAX_SIZE_GUESTUPLOAD: "1024"
      GOKAPI_MAX_FILES_GUESTUPLOAD: "10"
      GOKAPI_MIN_FREE_SPACE: "2048"
      GOKAPI_GUEST_UPLOAD_BY_DEFAULT: "false"
      GOKAPI_LOG_STDOUT: "true"
    volumes:
      - gokapi-config:/app/config
      - gokapi-data:/app/data
volumes:
  gokapi-config:
  gokapi-data:
```

`GOKAPI_MAX_FILESIZE` is in megabytes, so 4096 is a 4 GB ceiling per file. Pick a number with
the user; the default is 102400, which is 100 GB and more than twice the whole disk.
`GOKAPI_LOG_STDOUT` puts the log where `docker logs` can see it, which is where the
`--reconfigure` credentials appear later.

## The one that actually breaks it

**The first boot is an anonymous setup wizard.** Not a signup form: a wizard. Whoever completes it
chooses the database, the storage backend, the public URL, the encryption level **and** the
super-admin password. Until it is completed, every other path answers "Server is in maintenance
mode", and the container's own healthcheck reports the instance **healthy** the whole time.

There is no environment variable that closes this. `--deployment-password` only changes an
existing admin's password and then exits. The only thing that closes the window is completing the
wizard, which is why it is a script.

**And it can reopen.** Gokapi decides whether to run setup by asking whether its config file
exists. A redeploy without a real volume on `/app/config` comes back in first-run mode, wizard
open to the internet, with the files still sitting on the data volume.

## Claim the instance, and prove you did

Run this the moment the deploy reports ready, before the URL goes anywhere. Every field in the
payload was read out of `Setup.go` at tag v2.2.4; the wizard requires the keys for **all** auth
methods, not just the one being chosen, which is why the list is long.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Complete Gokapi's anonymous setup wizard and verify the result.
#   ./claim.sh gokapi-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud myusername
# Exit 0 = claimed and verified, 1 = FAILED (do not leave this instance up),
#          2 = inconclusive (it may still be starting; re-run).
set -eu
HOST="${1:?usage: claim.sh <host> <username>}"
GUSER="${2:?usage: claim.sh <host> <username>}"
TMP=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT

# 1. GATE. redu's proxy answers 502 for roughly the first 2.5 minutes while the container starts,
#    and an error page fails every assertion below in a way that reads like a pass. Require 200
#    AND require the string only an unconfigured Gokapi returns, before anything else runs.
code=$(curl -sSL -o "$TMP/root" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/")
if [ "$code" != "200" ]; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: / answered HTTP $code, not 200." >&2
  if [ "$code" = "502" ]; then
    echo "  502 is redu's proxy while the container starts. Wait and re-run. This is NOT a pass." >&2
  fi
  exit 2
fi
if ! grep -q 'maintenance mode' "$TMP/root"; then
  echo "FAIL: / returned 200 but not the setup-mode maintenance message." >&2
  echo "  Either somebody has ALREADY completed the wizard and owns this instance, or this is" >&2
  echo "  not Gokapi. Check by hand. Do not assume it is yours." >&2
  exit 1
fi
echo "OK: Gokapi is up and still in setup mode, so the wizard is unclaimed."

# 2. Confirm the wizard really is anonymous right now. 200 here is the POSITIVE result while
#    isInitialSetup is true; anything else means the state is not what this script expects.
scode=$(curl -sSL -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/setup/start")
[ "$scode" = "200" ] || { echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /setup/start answered $scode, expected 200." >&2; exit 2; }

# 3. CLAIM IT. Alphanumeric only, so there is nothing to escape in JSON or the shell.
#    The payload goes in from a file: an argument would show up in ps for every user here.
GPASS=[REDACTED:value] tr -dc 'A-Za-z0-9' < /dev/urandom | head -c 32)
cat > "$TMP/setup.json" <<EOF
[
 {"name":"dbtype_sel","value":"0"},
 {"name":"sqlite_location","value":"./data/gokapi.sqlite"},
 {"name":"redis_location","value":"127.0.0.1:6379"},
 {"name":"redis_prefix","value":""},
 {"name":"redis_user","value":""},
 {"name":"redis_password","value":""},
 {"name":"redis_ssl_sel","value":"0"},
 {"name":"authentication_sel","value":"0"},
 {"name":"auth_username","value":"$GUSER"},
 {"name":"auth_pw","value":"$GPASS"},
 {"name":"oauth_provider","value":""},
 {"name":"oauth_id","value":""},
 {"name":"oauth_secret","value":""},
 {"name":"oauth_recheck_interval","value":"12"},
 {"name":"oauth_admin_user","value":""},
 {"name":"oauth_only_registered_users","value":"0"},
 {"name":"oauth_restrict_groups","value":"0"},
 {"name":"oauth_allowed_groups","value":""},
 {"name":"oauth_scope_groups","value":""},
 {"name":"auth_header_admin","value":""},
 {"name":"auth_headerkey","value":""},
 {"name":"auth_header_only_registered_users","value":"0"},
 {"name":"port","value":"53842"},
 {"name":"localhost_sel","value":"0"},
 {"name":"public_name","value":"Gokapi"},
 {"name":"url","value":"https://$HOST/"},
 {"name":"url_redirection","value":"https://$HOST/login"},
 {"name":"ssl_sel","value":"0"},
 {"name":"logip_sel","value":"0"},
 {"name":"showfilename_sel","value":"0"},
 {"name":"storage_sel","value":"local"},
 {"name":"storage_sel_image","value":"local"},
 {"name":"storage_sel_proxy","value":"proxy"},
 {"name":"s3_bucket","value":""},
 {"name":"s3_region","value":""},
 {"name":"s3_api","value":""},
 {"name":"s3_secret","value":""},
 {"name":"s3_endpoint","value":""},
 {"name":"encrypt_sel","value":"0"},
 {"name":"enc_pw","value":""},
 {"name":"cleare2e","value":"0"}
]
EOF
code=$(curl -sS -o "$TMP/result" -w '%{http_code}' -X POST \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @"$TMP/setup.json" \
  "https://$HOST/setup/setupResult")
if [ "$code" != "200" ] || ! grep -q '"result": "OK"' "$TMP/result"; then
  echo "FAIL: the setup POST answered HTTP $code:" >&2
  cat "$TMP/result" >&2 || true
  echo >&2
  echo "  THE INSTANCE IS UNCLAIMED AND REACHABLE RIGHT NOW. Open https://$HOST/setup in a" >&2
  echo "  browser and finish the wizard THIS MINUTE, or delete the deployment. Gokapi answers" >&2
  echo "  with the name of the missing field, so a rejection here names what to add." >&2
  exit 1
fi
echo "OK: the wizard accepted the configuration."

# 4. The setup server shuts itself down about 1.5s later and the configured server starts.
#    Wait for it rather than guessing.
ready=0
for _ in $(seq 1 30); do
  sleep 3
  lcode=$(curl -sSL -o "$TMP/login" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/login" || true)
  if [ "$lcode" = "200" ] && grep -q 'csrf-token' "$TMP/login"; then ready=1; break; fi
done
[ "$ready" = "1" ] || { echo "INCONCLUSIVE: the configured server did not come up. Re-run." >&2; exit 2; }
echo "OK: the configured server is serving a login page."

# 5. PROVE THE OUTCOME, NOT THE STATUS CODE. A 200 from the wizard is not proof the password
#    works. A successful login answers 200 with a meta refresh to ./admin; a failure re-renders
#    the login form. The CSRF token is single use, so it is read from the page just fetched.
CSRF=$(sed -n 's/.*id="csrf-token"[^>]*value="\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p' "$TMP/login" | head -n1)
[ -n "$CSRF" ] || { echo "INCONCLUSIVE: no CSRF token in the login page." >&2; exit 2; }
code=$(curl -sS -o "$TMP/loggedin" -w '%{http_code}' -c "$TMP/jar" \
  --data-urlencode "username=$GUSER" --data-urlencode "password=[REDACTED:value]" \
  --data-urlencode "csrf-token=[REDACTED:value]" "https://$HOST/login")
if [ "$code" != "200" ] || ! grep -q 'URL=./admin' "$TMP/loggedin"; then
  echo "FAIL: signing in as $GUSER did not reach the admin page (HTTP $code)." >&2
  echo "  An account may exist with a credential you do not have. Do not leave this up." >&2
  exit 1
fi
echo "OK: signed in as $GUSER, so the account exists and the password works."

# 6. THE NEGATIVE HALF, which only means something because step 5 passed. The configured server
#    has no /setup route at all, so the wizard must now be gone.
scode=$(curl -sSL -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/setup/start")
if [ "$scode" = "200" ]; then
  echo "FAIL: /setup/start still answers 200. The wizard is STILL OPEN to anyone." >&2
  exit 1
fi
echo "OK: /setup/start is gone (HTTP $scode)."

echo
echo "CLAIMED. Admin user: $GUSER   (Gokapi lowercases it)"
echo "Password (shown once, store it now): $GPASS"
```

## Checking the volumes, which is what keeps the wizard shut

```bash
# On the VM, via get_ssh_command. Note redu's VMs run docker, not podman:
# a command that does not exist prints an error and greps to zero matches, which reads as a pass.
C=$(sudo docker ps --format '{{.Names}}' | grep -i gokapi | head -n1)
[ -n "$C" ] || { echo "no gokapi container found; nothing below means anything" >&2; exit 1; }

# Positive half: both mounts exist, and the config file that keeps setup closed is on one of them.
sudo docker inspect -f '{{range .Mounts}}{{.Destination}} {{end}}' "$C"
sudo docker exec "$C" ls -l /app/config/config.json /app/data/gokapi.sqlite

# Negative half: no database container is running alongside it. Only meaningful because the
# commands above just succeeded.
sudo docker ps --format '{{.Image}}' | grep -cE 'postgres|redis'

# And the number that decides whether this VM is the right size.
df -h /
```

I've read `redu.md`, checked prerequisites (account OK, network + keypair auto-selected), and planned the deploy. Plan written to `redu-deploy-plan.md`. **Nothing has been created yet.**

## Before the plan: the uncomfortable part

**This is a public file uploader on a `*.redu.cloud` hostname.** A file host that strangers can write to becomes a malware and phishing host within days of being found — and a safe-browsing or mail-provider blocklisting of `redu.cloud` lands on *every other customer* with a hostname on that domain, not just you. **You are responsible for whatever ends up on it**, including anything uploaded through a file request you hand out.

Gokapi is a reasonable shape for this because **there is no self-registration route at all** — accounts exist only because an admin creates them. But two things need naming:

- **The first boot is an anonymous setup wizard, not a login page.** Whoever completes it becomes super-admin and picks the database, storage backend, public URL and password. No env var closes it; the container reports *healthy* the entire time it sits open. I close it with the claim script from `redu.md` the second the deploy reports ready, then prove it's shut by logging in and confirming `/setup/start` is gone.
- **File requests** are the one anonymous write path — off by default, per-user permission. The moment you hand one out, this is a world-writable uploader. I'm capping guest uploads at 1 GB / 10 files.

## The plan

| | |
|---|---|
| **App** | Gokapi `f0rc3/gokapi:v2.2.4` (pinned), one container, port 53842 |
| **VM** | **m1.medium** — 2 vCPU / 4 GB / **40 GB disk** |
| **Database** | **None.** SQLite on the data volume — no second VM, no second bill line |
| **Volumes** | `gokapi-config:/app/config` + `gokapi-data:/app/data` |
| **Cost** | **GBP 0.0278/hr ≈ GBP 20.29/mo** — hourly, delete anytime, fits the no-card trial |

`plan_deploy` quoted **m1.large at GBP 35.48/mo** because declaring a compose stack raises the floor for apps that *build* from source. This one pulls a published image — a single small Go binary — so I'm holding m1.medium with `flavor_id "3"`, as `redu.md` records. That's ~43% cheaper.

**The disk is the real constraint.** All shared files live on that 40 GB, before Ubuntu, Docker and the image — plan on ~30 GB usable. Defaults I'm setting: **4 GB max per file** (the Gokapi default is 100 GB, more than twice the whole disk), 2 GB free-space floor, guest uploads off, **TZ=UTC**, and **downloader IP logging OFF** (upstream flags it as possibly not GDPR-compliant; wrong default for an EU-hosted service).

Expiry is the other half of the disk story — every share expires after N downloads or N days, set per upload. That's what keeps the disk from filling.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Complete Gokapi's anonymous setup wizard and verify the result.
#   ./claim.sh gokapi-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud myusername
# Exit 0 = claimed and verified, 1 = FAILED (do not leave this instance up),
#          2 = inconclusive (it may still be starting; re-run).
set -eu
HOST="${1:?usage: claim.sh <host> <username>}"
GUSER="${2:?usage: claim.sh <host> <username>}"
TMP=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT

# 1. GATE.
code=$(curl -sSL -o "$TMP/root" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/")
if [ "$code" != "200" ]; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: / answered HTTP $code, not 200." >&2
  if [ "$code" = "502" ]; then
    echo "  502 is redu's proxy while the container starts. Wait and re-run. This is NOT a pass." >&2
  fi
  exit 2
fi
if ! grep -q 'maintenance mode' "$TMP/root"; then
  echo "FAIL: / returned 200 but not the setup-mode maintenance message." >&2
  echo "  Either somebody has ALREADY completed the wizard and owns this instance, or this is" >&2
  echo "  not Gokapi. Check by hand. Do not assume it is yours." >&2
  exit 1
fi
echo "OK: Gokapi is up and still in setup mode, so the wizard is unclaimed."

# 2. Confirm the wizard really is anonymous right now.
scode=$(curl -sSL -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/setup/start")
[ "$scode" = "200" ] || { echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /setup/start answered $scode, expected 200." >&2; exit 2; }

# 3. CLAIM IT.
GPASS=[REDACTED:value] tr -dc 'A-Za-z0-9' < /dev/urandom | head -c 32)
cat > "$TMP/setup.json" <<EOF
[
 {"name":"dbtype_sel","value":"0"},
 {"name":"sqlite_location","value":"./data/gokapi.sqlite"},
 {"name":"redis_location","value":"127.0.0.1:6379"},
 {"name":"redis_prefix","value":""},
 {"name":"redis_user","value":""},
 {"name":"redis_password","value":""},
 {"name":"redis_ssl_sel","value":"0"},
 {"name":"authentication_sel","value":"0"},
 {"name":"auth_username","value":"$GUSER"},
 {"name":"auth_pw","value":"$GPASS"},
 {"name":"oauth_provider","value":""},
 {"name":"oauth_id","value":""},
 {"name":"oauth_secret","value":""},
 {"name":"oauth_recheck_interval","value":"12"},
 {"name":"oauth_admin_user","value":""},
 {"name":"oauth_only_registered_users","value":"0"},
 {"name":"oauth_restrict_groups","value":"0"},
 {"name":"oauth_allowed_groups","value":""},
 {"name":"oauth_scope_groups","value":""},
 {"name":"auth_header_admin","value":""},
 {"name":"auth_headerkey","value":""},
 {"name":"auth_header_only_registered_users","value":"0"},
 {"name":"port","value":"53842"},
 {"name":"localhost_sel","value":"0"},
 {"name":"public_name","value":"Gokapi"},
 {"name":"url","value":"https://$HOST/"},
 {"name":"url_redirection","value":"https://$HOST/login"},
 {"name":"ssl_sel","value":"0"},
 {"name":"logip_sel","value":"0"},
 {"name":"showfilename_sel","value":"0"},
 {"name":"storage_sel","value":"local"},
 {"name":"storage_sel_image","value":"local"},
 {"name":"storage_sel_proxy","value":"proxy"},
 {"name":"s3_bucket","value":""},
 {"name":"s3_region","value":""},
 {"name":"s3_api","value":""},
 {"name":"s3_secret","value":""},
 {"name":"s3_endpoint","value":""},
 {"name":"encrypt_sel","value":"0"},
 {"name":"enc_pw","value":""},
 {"name":"cleare2e","value":"0"}
]
EOF
code=$(curl -sS -o "$TMP/result" -w '%{http_code}' -X POST \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @"$TMP/setup.json" \
  "https://$HOST/setup/setupResult")
if [ "$code" != "200" ] || ! grep -q '"result": "OK"' "$TMP/result"; then
  echo "FAIL: the setup POST answered HTTP $code:" >&2
  cat "$TMP/result" >&2 || true
  echo >&2
  echo "  THE INSTANCE IS UNCLAIMED AND REACHABLE RIGHT NOW. Open https://$HOST/setup in a" >&2
  echo "  browser and finish the wizard THIS MINUTE, or delete the deployment. Gokapi answers" >&2
  echo "  with the name of the missing field, so a rejection here names what to add." >&2
  exit 1
fi
echo "OK: the wizard accepted the configuration."

# 4. Wait for the configured server.
ready=0
for _ in $(seq 1 30); do
  sleep 3
  lcode=$(curl -sSL -o "$TMP/login" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/login" || true)
  if [ "$lcode" = "200" ] && grep -q 'csrf-token' "$TMP/login"; then ready=1; break; fi
done
[ "$ready" = "1" ] || { echo "INCONCLUSIVE: the configured server did not come up. Re-run." >&2; exit 2; }
echo "OK: the configured server is serving a login page."

# 5. PROVE THE OUTCOME, NOT THE STATUS CODE.
CSRF=$(sed -n 's/.*id="csrf-token"[^>]*value="\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p' "$TMP/login" | head -n1)
[ -n "$CSRF" ] || { echo "INCONCLUSIVE: no CSRF token in the login page." >&2; exit 2; }
code=$(curl -sS -o "$TMP/loggedin" -w '%{http_code}' -c "$TMP/jar" \
  --data-urlencode "username=$GUSER" --data-urlencode "password=[REDACTED:value]" \
  --data-urlencode "csrf-token=[REDACTED:value]" "https://$HOST/login")
if [ "$code" != "200" ] || ! grep -q 'URL=./admin' "$TMP/loggedin"; then
  echo "FAIL: signing in as $GUSER did not reach the admin page (HTTP $code)." >&2
  echo "  An account may exist with a credential you do not have. Do not leave this up." >&2
  exit 1
fi
echo "OK: signed in as $GUSER, so the account exists and the password works."

# 6. THE NEGATIVE HALF.
scode=$(curl -sSL -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/setup/start")
if [ "$scode" = "200" ]; then
  echo "FAIL: /setup/start still answers 200. The wizard is STILL OPEN to anyone." >&2
  exit 1
fi
echo "OK: /setup/start is gone (HTTP $scode)."

echo
echo "CLAIMED. Admin user: $GUSER   (Gokapi lowercases it)"
echo "Password (shown once, store it now): $GPASS"
SCRIPT

---
redu_schema: 2
repo: https://github.com/Forceu/Gokapi
plan:
  tool: deploy_compose
  image: f0rc3/gokapi:v2.2.4
  port: 53842
  vm: m1.medium
  flavor_id: "3"
  database: none (SQLite on the data volume; do NOT provision a managed database)
  hourly_cost_gbp: 0.0278
bootstrap:
  mcp: claude mcp add --transport http redu «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --client-id redu-mcp
  mcp_codex: codex mcp add redu --url «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --oauth-client-id redu-mcp
  source: gokapi
quirks:
  - "⛔⛔ THIS IS A PUBLIC FILE UPLOADER, SO SAY THE UNCOMFORTABLE PART TO THE USER BEFORE YOU DEPLOY IT. Everything shared from here is served from a hostname under *.redu.cloud, and a file host that strangers can write to becomes a malware and phishing host within days of being found. That is not a risk to the operator alone: a blocklisting of redu.cloud by a browser safe-browsing list or a mail provider lands on EVERY other customer with a hostname on that domain. THE OPERATOR IS RESPONSIBLE FOR WHAT IS UPLOADED, including anything uploaded through a file request they hand out. Gokapi is a good shape for this, because it has no self-registration at all, but the operator still owns the consequences of every account and every file request they create."
  - "⛔⛔ WHO BECOMES THE ADMINISTRATOR, AND WHEN: THE FIRST VISITOR WHO FINISHES THE ANONYMOUS INSTALL WIZARD, AND ON FIRST BOOT THAT WIZARD IS THE ONLY THING RUNNING. Verified at Setup.go:60-65 and :83-90: when the config file does not exist Gokapi starts a BLOCKING setup webserver, and its basicAuth wrapper returns early with NO authentication while isInitialSetup is true. Every other path answers 'Server is in maintenance mode, please try again in a few minutes.' (Setup.go:111). One anonymous POST to /setup/setupResult writes the entire configuration, creates the super-admin with a password of the caller's choosing, and shuts the wizard down (Setup.go:784-806 via Configuration.go:135-160). That is worse than an unclaimed signup form: the caller also chooses the database, the storage backend, the public URL and the encryption level. THERE IS NO ENVIRONMENT VARIABLE THAT CLOSES THIS. --deployment-password only EDITS an existing super-admin and then exits (Configuration.go:192-206), and the wizard runs before it (Main.go:56-63). CLOSE THE WINDOW AS PART OF THE DEPLOY with the claim script in the body of this file, and if the script fails, finish the wizard in a browser IMMEDIATELY or delete the deployment."
  - "✅ THE CLAIM SCRIPT AND ITS PAYLOAD ARE CONFIRMED WORKING, VERBATIM, AT v2.2.4 (deployment 491, 2026-08-20). The 41-field JSON body in the body of this file was accepted on the first POST with no missing-field rejection, and all six assertions passed: maintenance string present -> /setup/start 200 -> setupResult '\"result\": \"OK\"' -> /login serving a csrf-token -> a real login reaching 'URL=./admin' -> /setup/start gone. THE EXACT AFTER-VALUE IS 404, so a future run can assert 404 rather than merely not-200. The whole claim took about 12 seconds once the host answered 200. Do not 'improve' the payload; it is field-complete as written."
  - "⏱️ TIMING, MEASURED: about 90 seconds from deploy_compose returning to the container being up, and HTTP 200 on the public hostname at roughly 1 minute 45 seconds. Before that the proxy answers 502 (7 consecutive 502s at 6-second intervals on deployment 491). The right shape is a poll loop that waits for 200 and then runs the claim script in the SAME command, so the unclaimed window is seconds rather than however long the agent takes to notice. Do not sit at a prompt between 'ready' and the claim."
  - "⚠️ A HEALTHY CONTAINER DOES NOT MEAN A CONFIGURED GOKAPI. The image's own HEALTHCHECK (Dockerfile:24) is curl --fail against http://127.0.0.1:53842, and during setup mode that path returns HTTP 200 with the maintenance message. So the container reports healthy while the instance is unclaimed and world-open. Never treat the container health, or redu reporting the deployment ready, as evidence that setup is done. The claim script gates on the maintenance string itself, which is the honest signal."
  - "✅ THE GOOD NEWS, AND IT IS THE REASON THIS APP IS A REASONABLE PUBLIC UPLOADER: THERE IS NO SELF-REGISTRATION ROUTE AT ALL. Webserver.go:103-132 is the complete route table of the configured server and contains no /register, no /signup and no /setup. Accounts exist only because an admin created one on the /users page. Upstream's own README puts it the same way: only registered users can upload. So once the super-admin is claimed, the door is shut permanently and there is no registration setting to remember to turn off."
  - "THE ONE ANONYMOUS WRITE PATH IS A FILE REQUEST, AND IT IS OPT-IN TWICE OVER. Webserver.go:963-983: /publicUpload needs BOTH a valid file request id AND a matching key, compared in constant time, and it refuses once the request has expired or hit its file limit. The right to create one is a per-user permission, and Environment.go:70 defaults GOKAPI_GUEST_UPLOAD_BY_DEFAULT to false, so only users an admin grants it to can hand out an upload URL. TELL THE USER IT EXISTS, because handing out a file request URL is exactly the moment this becomes a world-writable uploader, and GOKAPI_MAX_FILES_GUESTUPLOAD (default 100) and GOKAPI_MAX_SIZE_GUESTUPLOAD (default 10240, which the source comments as 10 GB) are the two numbers that bound the damage. Both are far too generous for a 40 GB disk."
  - "⛔⛔ MOUNT /app/config OR EVERY REDEPLOY REOPENS THE ANONYMOUS SETUP WIZARD ON A PUBLIC HOSTNAME. This is the highest-value line in this file and it is the local form of the usual secret-a-redeploy-destroys trap. Configuration.go:38-41 decides whether to run setup by asking one question: does the config file exist? So a container whose /app/config is not a real volume comes back from any redeploy in first-run mode, unauthenticated, with the setup wizard open to the internet, while the uploaded files sit on the data volume. The same file also holds SaltAdmin and SaltFiles, generated once at setup (Setup.go:388-404, toConfiguration at :236-300), which are what the stored admin password hash and every password-protected download link are salted with, plus the encryption cipher if encryption is on. Lose the file and you lose the logins, the protected links and the encrypted files even if you somehow re-ran setup safely. Mount BOTH /app/config and /app/data as named volumes, and check it after boot: Setup.go:750-760 reads /proc/mounts and the wizard itself warns when either is missing."
  - "THE VOLUME CHECK, WITH THE REAL NAMES: redu names the compose project app-src, so the container is app-src-gokapi-1 and the volumes come back from docker inspect as app-src_gokapi-config and app-src_gokapi-data, NOT the bare names in the compose file. Confirmed on deployment 491. A check that greps for the bare 'gokapi-config' still matches as a substring, but a check that compares for equality does not, and reads as a missing volume on a correctly mounted container."
  - "⛔ THE UPSTREAM COMPOSE PUBLISHES 127.0.0.1:53842:53842 AND ON redu THAT MEANS THE HOSTNAME NEVER WORKS.
